head.citation-title: Durability performance of soil concretes: Role of cement and soil types under carbonation and wetting/drying cycles
head.abstracts: © 2026 Elsevier LtdSoil concrete is a material obtained by mixing soil with cement. It is currently used for the construction of permanent structures such as dykes and retaining walls. The clay content in the soil requires a high-water content during preparation and placement, leading to increased porosity, which increases porosity and can negatively affect the long-term performance of soil concrete structures. In this context, it is essential to assess the durability of this material. Two durability indicators were studied in the laboratory: carbonation (mass loss (ζ), water-accessible porosity (η) and carbonation depth (Xc)) and wetting/drying (W/D) cycles (mass loss (ζ), P-wave velocity (Vp) and compressive strength (Rc)). The objective of this experimental study was to evaluate the role of cement and soil types on the durability performance of soil concretes under carbonation and W/D cycles. For the mixtures, two soils were selected: a clayey sand (SA5) and laterite (LA5), both with a grain size class of 0/5. Soil concretes were prepared at a constant spread of 32–33 cm (mini-slump test) using CEM I 52.5, CEM II 42.5, and CEM III 32.5 binders, with cement contents of 150 and 250 kg/m3. These durability tests were carried out on cylindrical specimens of dimensions (Ø = 60 mm and h = 120 mm) which were cured for 90 days in water prior to testing. The results indicate that mixtures containing CEM III 32.5 exhibited the highest carbonation depths due to the presence of blast-furnace slag, which reduces the availability of carbonatable products. LA5-based mixtures showed greater sensitivity to carbonation, mainly because of their higher porosity. While both soil and cement properties affect carbonation, the nature of the soil exerts a lesser influence on specimens containing Portland cements (CEM I 52.5 and CEM II 42.5) compared to those incorporating slag-based cement (CEM III 32.5). This can be explained by a soil-cement-water interaction. Unlike clinker, the main constituent of Portland cement, which hydrates faster, slag continues to hydrate over long periods. As our samples were cured for 90 days, this will lead to a more significant soil effect during carbonation in the case of formulations with CEM III 32.5 (blast furnace slag cement). Wetting/drying cycles led to higher mass losses and greater reductions in compressive strength in CEM III-based mixtures, particularly those prepared with LA5 soil. This behavior is attributed to the delayed hydraulic reactivity of slag, which causes mechanical instability during cyclic exposure. Overall, the study demonstrates that both cement composition and soil characteristics play a key role in controlling the durability of soil concrete under environmental actions.

coredata.dc:description: Soil concrete is a material obtained by mixing soil with cement. It is currently used for the construction of permanent structures such as dykes and retaining walls. The clay content in the soil requires a high-water content during preparation and placement, leading to increased porosity, which increases porosity and can negatively affect the long-term performance of soil concrete structures. In this context, it is essential to assess the durability of this material. Two durability indicators were studied in the laboratory: carbonation (mass loss (ζ), water-accessible porosity (η) and carbonation depth (Xc)) and wetting/drying (W/D) cycles (mass loss (ζ), P-wave velocity (Vp) and compressive strength (Rc)). The objective of this experimental study was to evaluate the role of cement and soil types on the durability performance of soil concretes under carbonation and W/D cycles. For the mixtures, two soils were selected: a clayey sand (SA5) and laterite (LA5), both with a grain size class of 0/5. Soil concretes were prepared at a constant spread of 32–33 cm (mini-slump test) using CEM I 52.5, CEM II 42.5, and CEM III 32.5 binders, with cement contents of 150 and 250 kg/m3. These durability tests were carried out on cylindrical specimens of dimensions (Ø = 60 mm and h = 120 mm) which were cured for 90 days in water prior to testing. The results indicate that mixtures containing CEM III 32.5 exhibited the highest carbonation depths due to the presence of blast-furnace slag, which reduces the availability of carbonatable products. LA5-based mixtures showed greater sensitivity to carbonation, mainly because of their higher porosity. While both soil and cement properties affect carbonation, the nature of the soil exerts a lesser influence on specimens containing Portland cements (CEM I 52.5 and CEM II 42.5) compared to those incorporating slag-based cement (CEM III 32.5). This can be explained by a soil-cement-water interaction. Unlike clinker, the main constituent of Portland cement, which hydrates faster, slag continues to hydrate over long periods. As our samples were cured for 90 days, this will lead to a more significant soil effect during carbonation in the case of formulations with CEM III 32.5 (blast furnace slag cement). Wetting/drying cycles led to higher mass losses and greater reductions in compressive strength in CEM III-based mixtures, particularly those prepared with LA5 soil. This behavior is attributed to the delayed hydraulic reactivity of slag, which causes mechanical instability during cyclic exposure. Overall, the study demonstrates that both cement composition and soil characteristics play a key role in controlling the durability of soil concrete under environmental actions.
coredata.dc:title: Durability performance of soil concretes: Role of cement and soil types under carbonation and wetting/drying cycles
